summary: Kojun Saito (1930–2002) worked in Buddhist studies and Indology. He studied under Seiren Matsunami (attested 1977) and served as a lecturer at Taisho University (attested 1965).
Kokan Fujita (b. 1944) is a Buddhist studies scholar who studied under Yujun Endo. He served as a professor at Koyasan University (attested 1995–2002).

Koken Sasaki (1931–2008) studied at Rissho University (~1950–1960). In Buddhist studies and Sinology, he served at Rissho as assistant professor (~1968–1975), department head (~1975–2001), professor/director (attested 2000), and professor emeritus (~2001–2008).
Koki Kawagishi (1928–2011) was a Buddhist studies scholar. In 1976, he is attested holding professor posts at both Eizan Gakuin and Shitennoji University.

Komal Asrani works in computational Indology. After studying at Government Engineering College and earning a Ph.D. from Uttar Pradesh Rajarshi Tandon Open University (2002–2005), Asrani held a computer science post at Babu Banarasi Das Group in 2006.
Konchok Drakpa studied under Patrul Rinpoche and Jamgon Ju Mipham Gyatso, and went on to teach Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche.
Konchok Gyatso is a Tibetology scholar who studied under Sherab Gyatso. He held an attested post at the Tibet Academy of Social Sciences in 2014.
Konchok Zangpo was a student of both Patrul Rinpoche and Jamgon Ju Mipham Gyatso.

Konrad Gottlob Anton (1745–1814) was a linguistics and Indology scholar. He studied at the University of Leipzig (~1763–1770) and was appointed Professor of Oriental and Classical Languages at the University of Wittenberg in 1775.
Konrad Ihlefeld (1837–1906) was a scholar of Indology and linguistics. He studied at the University of Rostock in 1858 and served as director of Porayar Seminary from 1878 to 1885.

Konrad Klaus (b. 1956), an Indologist and Tibetologist, studied at Göttingen, Marburg, and under Wilhelm Rau and Michael Hahn. He held substitute professorships at Bochum, Marburg, and Bonn (1999–2001) before succeeding Claus Vogel in 2001.
Konrad Meisig (b. 1953) is a scholar in Indology and Buddhist studies. He studied under Ulrich Schneider (~1978–1986) and held a post at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (~1990–2019).

Kosaku Hamada (1881–1938) worked in history, archaeology, Sinology, and Japanology. He studied at the University of Tokyo (~1902–1905), later holding posts there (~1909–1913) and at Kyoto University (~1913–1938).

Kosei Ishii (b. 1950) studied at Waseda under Akira Hirakawa. Specializing in Buddhist studies and philosophy, he held posts at Waseda, Komazawa Junior College (1994–2006), and Komazawa University (~1994; emeritus 2006–2021).

Kosei Tada (1938–2017) was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at the University of Tokyo (~1961–1970). He held a post at Taisho University (~1975–2009) and served as board chairman of the Society for Buddhist Cultural Studies (attested 2004).
Koshin Suzuki (b. 1959) is an Indology and Buddhist studies scholar. He completed doctoral studies at Taisho University, where he also served as a researcher (attested 1995–1998).

Koshiro Tamaki (1915–1999) worked in Buddhist studies, Indology, and philosophy. He studied at the Fifth Higher School and University of Tokyo, later holding professorships at Tokyo (1964–1976), Tohoku (~1976–1979), and Nihon University (1979–1986).

Kosho Kawamura (b. 1924) studied at Toyo University under Giyu Nishi, Nichijin Sakamoto, Shunkyo Katsumata, Koshiro Tamaki, and Yoshiro Tamura. He held posts at Toyo (~1957–1995), Minobusan University (attested 1996), and Nava Nalanda Mahavihara (attested 2001).

Kosho Mizutani (1928–2014) was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at Ryukoku and Bukkyo universities. He served at Bukkyo University as assistant professor (~1962–1971) and president (~1979–1991), and chaired Bukkyo Kyoiku Gakuen (~1991–2011) and Tokai Gakuen (~2004–2014).

Kosho Uchiyama (1912–1998) studied Western philosophy at Waseda and trained under Kodo Sawaki. Working in Buddhist studies and philosophy, he taught at Miyazaki Catholic Seminary (~1937–1940) and succeeded Sawaki as abbot of Antai-ji (1965–1975).
